name: Kira Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm head of buying for furniture and homewares at Coastline Hospitality Supply. We equip hotels, guesthouses and restaurants, so I buy beds, chairs, crockery and linen from factories in Portugal, Vietnam and Turkey. Most days I'm reading samples reports, comparing quotes in a spreadsheet and sitting in meetings with the sales team about what the hotels want next season. Twice a year I travel to factories to check quality, which I enjoy more than I admit.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: What I like is that it's a mix of taste and arithmetic. I get to say that a chair feels cheap even though the numbers look good. What wears me out is the amount of chasing: late shipments, wrong colours, customs delays. My husband Anwar, a civil engineer at the water company, says I run my life from a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. I call this one "AI Plateau". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible to stay level-headed. At work I'd say use it where it helps and ignore the noise. To friends I'd say they'll hear a lot more about it than they'll see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be fine. I'm senior, well paid and good at the part that needs judgement, which is knowing what a hotel guest will sit on for ten years. I'd be glad if AI took over some of the admin chasing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, and gradually use it a bit more for what it's good at: translating supplier emails and summarising contracts. I'd keep to my plan to work until 63 and keep adding to the pension. I'd also keep up the factory visits, which keep me credible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I have a decent cushion and a job I can do in my sleep, and there's no drama.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay calm. What would you say is secure and what isn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Secure: money, standing, and the fact that I'm good. Not entirely secure: the hotel trade swings with tourism, and a bad season hurts us. And my father is unwell, so I'm often on the road to see him, which strains my week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you use AI tools today, and would that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use it now and then, to summarise a long contract or to draft a polite reply in Portuguese. I check the result every time, since it once translated a delivery term wrongly. If it keeps improving I'll use it more, but I wait until the others have shaken out the bugs.

say: I'd say stay **level-headed**: use AI where it helps and ignore the noise.
To friends I'd say they'll hear more about it than they'll see.
think: Privately I'm fine: I'm senior, and strong on **judgement** about what guests will sit on.
I'd welcome AI taking over some of the **admin chasing**.
do: Use AI a little more for **translation** and contract summaries, always checking the result.
Keep working to **63**, adding to the pension and visiting factories.
feel: **Calm**: a decent cushion and a job I can do in my sleep.
S0.quote: I use it now and then, to summarise a long contract or to draft a polite reply in Portuguese.
fieldNote: Calm is **earned**: money, standing and a judgement-heavy job.
Her pressures are tourism swings and a sick father, not AI.
Checks every AI output after a mistranslated delivery term.

steps.text: Use AI for contract summaries and Portuguese emails, checking each
Keep adding to the pension toward retiring at 63

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. I call this one "Steady Disruption". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it will change a lot of the routine, and we should prepare. At work I'd propose we pick two tasks to hand to software on purpose, rather than wait for a mandate. Online I'd say it's neither a disaster nor a gift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, quotes, comparisons and reorders go first. That's probably 60 per cent of the day for the junior buyers, and maybe 40 per cent for me. The taste and the supplier trust part remains, but a hotel chain could decide it can live with a standard catalogue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a proper course on AI tools in the spring and ask Coastline to pay. I'd move my two junior buyers onto supplier audits and design briefs, and let software do the quotes. And I'd start keeping a file of the relationships and judgement calls that only I know, which makes me harder to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job is probably safe, but I'm watching how the ground moves around me, and I notice it's on my mind more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of buying would move to software first in your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quotes first, then the reorders, then the tracking of shipments. The thing that stays is the awkward call when a factory gets the colour wrong and you have to decide whether to refuse the batch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask Coastline to do if it cut buying roles?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for no compulsory redundancies for two years, a retraining budget, and a clear statement of what roles will exist. Coastline can afford it, and it keeps good people. I'd say it as a business case, not a plea.

say: I'd say it will change much of the routine, so we should **pick two tasks** to hand to software on purpose.
Online I'd say it's neither disaster nor gift.
think: Privately **quotes and reorders** go first, about 60 per cent of the junior buyers' day.
My job is probably safe, but a hotel chain could accept a **standard catalogue**.
do: Take a proper **AI course** in spring and ask Coastline to pay.
Move two junior buyers to **supplier audits** and design briefs, and keep a file of my judgement calls.
feel: **Uneasy**: probably safe, but it's on my mind more than before.
S1.quote: The thing that stays is the awkward call when a factory gets the colour wrong and you have to decide whether to refuse the batch.
fieldNote: Sees buying as **taste plus trust**, with taste harder to automate.
Makes the retraining request as a business case.
Protective of junior buyers but not emotional about it.

steps.text: Take a paid AI course in spring
Move junior buyers onto supplier audits and design briefs
Ask Coastline for two years without forced redundancies
Keep a file of supplier relationships and judgement calls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. I call this one "AGI by 2028". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's moving faster than any of us can handle, and we need decisions by governments. At work I'd stay open and tell people what I know. Online I'd keep to facts and avoid panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think my role goes. If AI can do any thinking job as well, choosing furniture for a hotel is something it would learn from the images and the sales data. I'd be 60 and out of work, but with savings. The scary part is how many people I know are in the same boat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd first check our money with Anwar, then talk to Coastline about a package. I'd stop big spending, such as the kitchen refit we've been planning. I'd also look at a part-time role in design consulting, using my eye for furniture, which is probably the last bit to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd have the means, but I'd not know what my days were for. And I'd worry about Samira and Imran starting their careers into this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In two years, what would the fall-out be for Anwar and your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anwar's work is on pipes, pumps and drains. Some of it moves to software, but concrete and mud need people for years. So he's the stable one. Samira is a junior doctor, which is safe for a while, and Imran teaches in a primary school. We'd be okay, I think, but our world will shake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do first, and what would you leave alone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd leave alone the pension and the house, because panic selling is the way people lose money. I'd go ahead with the plans for Samira's wedding, which is next year. I wouldn't cancel a happy thing because of a headline.

say: I'd say it's **faster** than any of us can handle, and governments must decide.
Online I'd stick to facts and avoid panic.
think: Privately I think my role **goes**, as AI could learn furniture choices from images and sales data.
I'd be 60 and out of work, but with **savings**.
do: Check our **money** with Anwar, talk to Coastline about a package and shelve the kitchen refit.
Look at **part-time design consulting** and keep Samira's wedding plans.
feel: **Anxious**: I'd have the means but not know what my days are for.
S2.quote: I wouldn't cancel a happy thing because of a headline.
fieldNote: Sees Anwar's civil engineering work as the household's stable anchor.
She refuses to panic-sell, and keeps her daughter's wedding plans going.

steps.text: Check savings and pension with Anwar this month
Offer part-time design consulting to small hotels
Keep Samira's wedding plans for next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. I call this one "AGI by 2031". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long enough run to prepare, if we're honest and use it. At work I'd put together a plan to move the team towards supplier relations and design. Online I'd say the question is who pays for the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's more manageable. I'd be 63 and could stop on my terms. But Imran and Samira would be at the start of their careers, so I'd worry about them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a small design consultancy for independent hotels in the evenings, to test it while I still have the day job. I'd save harder for the first three years and delay the kitchen refit. And I'd train the junior buyers to be the human face of buying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It would be on my mind but not keeping me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, what would you start straight away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd regret not trying the consultancy early, and not spending time with my father while I can. Five years lets me do both, if I'm disciplined. Two years wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd regret not doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as two years but slower: I'd leave the house, the pension and my friendships alone. I'd put effort where it creates options, such as a new skill and a side client. That's the sensible way.

say: I'd say it's a long enough run to prepare, and the question is **who pays**.
At work I'd move the team towards supplier relations and design.
think: Privately it's more manageable: I'd be **63** and could stop on my terms.
I'd still worry about Samira and Imran at the **start of their careers**.
do: Start a small **design consultancy** for independent hotels in the evenings.
Save harder for three years and train juniors to be the **human face** of buying.
feel: **Uneasy**, on my mind but not keeping me up.
S3.quote: I'd put effort where it creates options, such as a new skill and a side client.
fieldNote: Five years let her **test** a second career while she still has her job.
Wants to spend time with her father while she can.
Prudent, with no appetite for dramatic moves.

steps.text: Start a design consultancy for independent hotels in evenings
Save harder for three years and delay the refit
Train junior buyers to be the human face of buying

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. I call this one "AGI by 2036". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to be sensible, and no need to rush. At work I'd say keep learning. Online I'd say the key question is training for young people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be retired and fine. It's Samira and Imran I think about. I'd want them to be in work that needs a person, which is why I'm glad Samira's a doctor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working until 63 and do some consulting for a few years after. I'd use the extra savings to help Samira and Imran with deposits, and put the rest in a spread of funds. And I'd travel with Anwar, since he's wanted to see the Lofoten islands for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Not smug, but settled. It's far enough off that I can enjoy my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A decade is a different animal. How much should anyone plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, and not everything. I'd keep skills fresh and savings healthy, and keep an eye out each year. A big plan for ten years out is a fantasy, because nobody knows how it unfolds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you want for your children, looking at that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want them to have jobs they can be proud of, enough money, and a good community. I'd tell them to learn the tools and to learn how to talk to people. Those are the ones that won't date.

say: I'd say there's **time to be sensible**, with no need to rush.
Online I'd say the key issue is **training** for young people.
think: Privately I'd be retired and fine, so I think about **Samira and Imran**.
I'm glad Samira is a doctor, a job that **needs a person**.
do: Work to **63**, then do some consulting for a few years.
Help both children with **deposits** and take Anwar to the Lofoten islands.
feel: **Calm** and settled, as it's far enough off to enjoy my life.
S4.quote: A big plan for ten years out is a fantasy, because nobody knows how it unfolds.
fieldNote: The **distance** brings real calm, and she is not smug about it.
Advice to children: tools plus people skills.
Measured in tone, and wary of big plans for a world no one can predict.

steps.text: Work to 63 then do some consulting
Help Samira and Imran with deposits

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me most. It gives no time to find a second thing to do, and it lands on everyone at once. What would help is a firm notice period, some help with retraining, and a pension that stays safe. I'd also like honest information from the company about what roles will exist.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I don't think people like me should be told to 'embrace change' as if it's a hobby. Some of us are cautious because we have a lot to protect, and that is not a fault.

headlineQuote: Some of us are cautious because we have a lot to protect, and that is not a fault.
portrait: Kira is a **58-year-old** head of buying for furniture and homewares at a hospitality supplier, and uses AI tools now and then.
She is a steady centrist, who mixes taste and arithmetic, and checks every AI output after a costly mistranslation.
Her mood moves from calm to **anxious** as the timeline shortens, mostly about purpose and her children's start in work.
She blames no one, wants honest information, and refuses to panic-sell.
A civil-engineer husband and savings let her test a **design consultancy** and help her children.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most, because it leaves no time to find a second thing to do.
whatWouldHelp: A firm **notice period**, retraining help, a safe pension and honest information from the company about future roles.
